name: Adam Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, and your name won't be attached to any of it. Could you start by telling me a little about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Adam, 27, and I'm in my first year as a qualified nurse, on the respiratory ward at Northgate Hospital. Before nursing I spent six years in a parcel warehouse, lifting boxes and living with my mum, which is the only reason I've got any savings. I live with my partner Luis, who teaches at a primary school, in a rented flat on Albion Street.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a normal working day look like for you? What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm mostly on nights, so I start at eight in the evening with handover and finish at eight in the morning. It's oxygen levels, nebulisers, people with COPD, which is a long-term lung disease, and people with pneumonia who suddenly get worse at three in the morning. I love the quiet hours when you can actually talk to someone who can't sleep. What wears me out is the fluid charts and the paperwork, and the fact that I'm still slower than the nurses who've done this for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, good, now let's spend the money on beds instead. On nights we've got two nurses and a healthcare assistant for twenty-four patients, half of them on oxygen. I'd probably share a post about that rather than about AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, a bit of me would be disappointed. I've used a chatbot to double-check a drug dose at three in the morning when the pharmacist wasn't answering, and it helped. If that's all it ever does, fine, but I'd hoped it would take the fluid charts off us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my nights on the respiratory ward and finish my preceptorship properly, which is the supported first year for new nurses. I'd keep putting a bit aside each month like I always do. Luis and I want to buy somewhere in two years, so the savings stay put.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly let down, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hoped AI would take the fluid charts. Why those?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because at four in the morning I'm adding up how many millilitres went in and out of twelve people with a biro, and I make mistakes. A machine could do sums better than a tired man on his fourth night. I'd rather spend those twenty minutes checking whether Mr Haddad in bed nine can actually breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything about money on your mind in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. I've got about nine months of wages put by from the warehouse years, and there are nursing jobs all over this city. The only money worry is house prices, and that's not an AI thing.

say: I'd say the money should go on **more beds and nurses** instead of software.
I'd post about **night staffing**, two nurses for twenty-four patients, rather than about AI.
think: I'd be a little **disappointed**, because a chatbot has helped me check doses at night.
I'd hoped AI would take the **fluid charts**, where tired nurses make sum errors.
do: Finish my **preceptorship year** on nights on the respiratory ward.
Keep saving each month toward a **house with Luis** in two years.
feel: **Calm**, with nine months saved and plenty of nursing jobs nearby.
Slightly **let down** that the useful tools never came.
S0.quote: A machine could do sums better than a tired man on his fourth night.
fieldNote: He already uses a **chatbot** for dose checks when the pharmacist can't be reached.
His **warehouse years** gave him savings and a practical eye on machines.
His only money worry is **house prices**, which he keeps separate from AI.

steps.text: Finish the first-year preceptorship on the respiratory night shift
Put money aside monthly toward a house deposit with his partner

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be good for nurses if we make sure the time saved comes back to patients. I've seen what happens otherwise: at the warehouse they brought in scanners that told you the fastest route, and then they just raised the targets. I'd say that at work and in the union chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my own job is safe. A respiratory patient at night needs someone to notice their lips going blue, and software doesn't stand at the bedside. What I worry about is Luis, because a lot of a teacher's day is planning and marking, and that's exactly what this picture describes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new charting tools once the early wards have ironed out the bugs, and I'd use them. I'd go to a union meeting for the first time in ages to ask how the saved time will be protected. And Luis and I would keep the deposit money where it is rather than buying sooner, until we see what happens to schools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly for Luis. For me it feels manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait for the early wards to iron out the bugs. Why not be first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've been first before. At the warehouse I volunteered for the new pick system and spent a month being blamed for its mistakes. I'd let the keen ones go first and then copy them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Luis if his school started cutting planning time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him not to panic, because kids still need an adult in the room. But I'd also say, maybe look at the specialist roles, the ones working with children who need extra support. I'd rather we talked about it early than at the kitchen table in a crisis.

say: I'd say AI helps nurses only if **saved time** goes back to patients.
I'd warn colleagues that my old warehouse just **raised targets** after new scanners.
think: My own **bedside job** is safe, because software can't spot blue lips at night.
I worry about **Luis**, since planning and marking are a teacher's thinking work.
do: Learn the **charting tools** once early wards have fixed the bugs.
Go to a **union meeting** to ask how saved time is protected.
Hold the **house deposit** until we see what happens to schools.
feel: **Uneasy**, mostly on behalf of Luis and his school job.
**Manageable** when I think only about my own ward.
S1.quote: At the warehouse they brought in scanners that told you the fastest route, and then they just raised the targets.
fieldNote: He expects his own job is safe but worries about his **partner's teaching**.
His warehouse past makes him wary of **targets** rising after new tools arrive.
He'd **follow, not lead**, after being blamed for a pilot system's errors before.

steps.text: Start using the charting tools once other wards have fixed the bugs
Attend a union meeting about protecting time saved by AI
Delay buying a house until schools' plans for teachers are clear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments need to move now, this year, on income support and retraining, because two years is nothing. I'd be at every union meeting and I'd write to my local representative. Online I'd probably share the warehouse story again, because I've seen how fast a place can empty out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think Luis's job is the one in danger first. If AI can plan lessons and mark and explain things better than a person by 2028, schools will want fewer teachers. My job gets about three extra years, until robots can roll people and suction a chest, and even then I think they'd keep some of us, but juniors like me are the cheapest to drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and push hard to get onto the high dependency side of the ward, because sicker patients are the last thing anyone automates. Luis and I would put the house on hold and keep all the savings in an easy-access account. I'd take more night shifts in the first year to build the cushion, because nights pay extra.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's the first time I'd feel like our whole household could be on one income, and that income is mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep the savings easy to reach. What does that mean for the two of you, day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means no house, no new car, and probably no big holiday. We'd stay in the rented flat on Albion Street. If Luis lost his job, I'd want to be able to cover his half for a year without blinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned juniors are the cheapest to drop. Do you think about that a lot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On nights, yes. When the robots come, they'll keep the experienced nurses to supervise them, and people like me are still learning. So the next three years matter, because by 2031 I need to be someone the hospital can't easily let go.

say: I'd say governments must act **this year** on income support and retraining.
I'd **write to my representative** and share how fast my old warehouse emptied.
think: **Luis's teaching job** is in danger first, once AI can plan and mark by 2028.
My job gets **three extra years**, but juniors are the cheapest to drop.
do: Push to move onto the **high dependency** side of the respiratory ward.
Put the **house on hold** and keep savings in an easy-access account.
Pick up **extra night shifts** in the first year to grow the cushion.
feel: **Anxious**, picturing our whole household living on my one income.
S2.quote: By 2031 I need to be someone the hospital can't easily let go.
fieldNote: His worry centres on his **partner's job**, which faces thinking AI first.
He clearly sees the **three-year gap** before robots reach bedside care.
He's planning to **cover Luis's half** of the costs for a year if needed.
He feels his **junior status** makes him exposed once robots arrive.

steps.text: Apply for a place on the high dependency side of the ward
Work extra paid night shifts to grow the savings
Put the house purchase on hold and keep renting on Albion Street
Write to his local representative about income support and retraining

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get it right if people start now: retraining money, rules on staffing, proper support for anyone whose job goes. I'd be one of the people saying that in the union chat. I'd sound less urgent than with the two-year one, but not by much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years suits me better than it suits Luis, but it gives us both a chance. He'd have time to move into special needs teaching or something more hands-on, and I'd have time to get properly good. By 2034 I'd be thirty-five, with eight years of nursing behind me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a respiratory nursing course next year, things like managing patients on breathing machines, and I'd use the AI tools at work once they're proven on other wards. We'd still buy a house, just a smaller one, maybe in Eastfield where it's cheaper. And I'd keep a year of wages in the bank no matter what.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but with a plan. More like a long to-do list than a fire alarm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd still buy a house. Isn't that a risk with robots coming in 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But nurses will be needed somewhere in 2034 even if it's fewer of us. I'd rather own a small house than rent forever, and keep the mortgage low enough that one of us could pay it alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the student nurses on your ward in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say learn the hard clinical stuff, ventilators, deteriorating patients, end of life, because the easy tasks will go first. And I'd tell them to join the union on day one. Nobody told me that, and I wish someone had.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough if retraining and staffing rules start now.
I'd push that message in the **union chat**, a little less urgently.
think: **Five years** gives Luis time to move into more hands-on teaching.
By **2034** I'd have eight years of nursing behind me.

Buy a **smaller house** in Eastfield with a mortgage one wage can cover.
Keep **a year of wages** in the bank whatever happens.
feel: **Uneasy**, but it feels like a long to-do list, not a fire alarm.
S3.quote: I'd rather own a small house than rent forever, and keep the mortgage low enough that one of us could pay it alone.
fieldNote: The extra time lets him **plan for two careers**, not just his own.
He'd still buy a house, but **sized to one income**.
His advice to students is to master **hard clinical skills** and join a union early.

steps.text: Enrol on a respiratory nursing course covering ventilated patients
Use AI charting tools once other wards have proven them
Buy a smaller house in Eastfield with a one-wage mortgage
Keep a full year of wages in an easy-access account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning, and if we can't prepare in ten years that's on the people in charge. I'd tell friends to treat it like a pension: start now, a bit at a time. I wouldn't be shouting about it online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this is the version where I think we'd be fine. By 2039 I'd be a senior respiratory nurse, the kind who runs the robots instead of being replaced by them. And Luis has a whole decade to shift towards work with kids that needs a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the respiratory course, then maybe a degree top-up over a few years. We'd buy the house in two years like we planned. I'd use the AI tools as they become normal, same as everyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. There's a small worry in the back of my head, but it's quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said juniors are the cheapest to drop. Why doesn't that bother you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because in ten years I won't be a junior nurse anymore, and that's the whole difference between the two-year picture and this one. Time turns me from the person they let go into the person who trains the people after me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything you'd do differently with the money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe put a little into a pension earlier than I would have. Luis's dad always says start at twenty-five, and we're both already late. But no big changes.

I'd tell friends to treat it like a **pension**: start now, bit by bit.

Luis has a **decade** to move toward teaching work that needs a person.

Buy the **house** in two years, as planned.

S4.quote: In ten years I won't be a junior nurse anymore, and that's the whole difference between the two-year picture and this one.
fieldNote: For him, **time changes status**: from cheap junior to the one who trains others.
Ten years removes most of his worry about **Luis's job**.
His plans barely change; he adds an **earlier pension** and a degree top-up.

steps.text: Finish the respiratory course, then start a part-time degree top-up

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it hits Luis first and me three years later, so there's no breathing space for either of us. What would help is income support for teachers and nurses while they retrain, paid properly, not some form that takes six months. And a staffing law, so the robots add to the ward instead of replacing the night nurse.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about partners. Everyone asks about my job, but our household is two jobs, and the risk is really about the pair of us. I've watched couples at the warehouse fall apart when one of them got laid off.

headlineQuote: Everyone asks about my job, but our household is two jobs, and the risk is really about the pair of us.
portrait: Adam, 27, is a **junior night nurse** on a respiratory ward, still in his first supported year.
Six years in a **parcel warehouse** left him savings and a wary eye on new tools.
He lives with Luis, a **primary teacher**, and they're saving for a house.
He feels his own job is fairly safe, but fears AI hits **Luis's teaching** first.
Time is everything for him: ten years turns a **cheap junior** into a senior nurse.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his partner is hit in 2028 and he follows by 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Income support** for teachers and nurses while they retrain, paid quickly.
A **staffing law** so robots add to night shifts rather than replace nurses.
